subtopics.title: Hydrosphere and the water cycle
subtopics.theory_md: The **hydrosphere** is all the water of the Earth: oceans, seas, rivers, lakes, groundwater, ice and water vapour. Oceans hold about **97%**; fresh water is only about **2.5%**, and of that roughly **69% is locked in ice caps and glaciers**, about 30% is groundwater and under 1% is in rivers, lakes and air. Water moves by the **hydrological cycle**: evaporation and transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff and infiltration, back to the sea. The cycle is driven by solar energy and renews fresh water.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of all the water on Earth as one tank that is only ever moved around. The sun lifts water from the sea, wind carries it over land, rain drops it, rivers carry it back. Very little of it is drinkable and easy to reach.
key_points: Hydrosphere = all water: ocean, fresh water, groundwater, ice, vapour
Oceans about 97%; fresh water about 2.5%
Most fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers
Hydrological cycle driven by solar energy: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff

questions.q: Define hydrosphere. Describe the hydrological cycle in short and say why fresh water is a scarce resource.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Hydrosphere:** the total water of the Earth in all forms: oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, ice and vapour.

**Hydrological cycle (driven by solar energy):**
1. Evaporation from oceans and transpiration from plants.
2. Condensation of vapour into clouds.
3. Precipitation as rain or snow.
4. Runoff to rivers and infiltration to groundwater, returning to the sea.

**Scarcity:** oceans are about 97% (saline); of the 2.5% fresh water about 69% is in ice and about 30% is deep groundwater, so under 1% of fresh water is easily usable.
points: Hydrosphere defined as all water of the Earth
Cycle steps: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff/infiltration
Solar energy is the driver
Fresh water only about 2.5%, most of it frozen or deep, so scarce

subtopics.title: Why water is special
subtopics.theory_md: Water is a **polar** molecule with a high **dielectric constant (about 78)**, so it pulls apart and dissolves ionic compounds and polar molecules such as glucose. This lets it carry mineral nutrients ($\mathrm{K^+, Ca^{2+}, NO_3^-, PO_4^{3-}}$) to cells and carry away ionic wastes in urine and sweat. Hydrogen bonding gives a **high specific heat and latent heat**, so oceans and organisms resist temperature change; a boiling point of 100 °C keeps body fluid from evaporating; **ice floats**, so lakes freeze from the top and life survives below. Cohesion and adhesion lift sap in trees.
subtopics.basics_md: Water molecules are a bit like tiny magnets with a positive and a negative end. That is why salt falls apart in water: the ends grab the ions. Acetone has a much weaker grip.
key_points: Polar molecule with high dielectric constant (about 78): dissolves ionic compounds
Carries nutrients to cells and removes ionic wastes
High specific and latent heat: stabilises climate and body temperature
Ice floats, so aquatic life survives under frozen lakes

subtopics.title: The cryosphere and climate
subtopics.theory_md:
The **cryosphere** is the frozen part of the Earth: ice sheets (Greenland, Antarctica), glaciers, sea ice, snow cover and permafrost. It regulates climate by:
1. **Albedo:** snow and ice reflect 80-90% of sunlight (open ocean about 6-10%); melting exposes dark surfaces, so more heat is absorbed and more ice melts (**ice-albedo feedback**).
2. **Sea level:** ice sheets store about 69% of fresh water.
3. **Ocean circulation:** sea-ice formation makes cold, dense, salty water that drives thermohaline circulation.
4. **Permafrost carbon:** thawing releases $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{CH_4}$.
5. Glaciers feed rivers such as the Ganga and Indus.
subtopics.basics_md: Snow is white and bounces sunlight back to space. When it melts, dark ground or sea shows up, takes in the heat and melts even more snow. That loop is why ice matters for climate.
key_points: Cryosphere = ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, snow, permafrost
High albedo reflects sunlight; melting gives positive feedback
Stores about 69% of fresh water; melting raises sea level
Sea ice drives ocean circulation; permafrost thaw releases CO2 and CH4

questions.model_answer_md:

2. **Sea-ice loss:** the bright ice (albedo 80-90%) is replaced by dark ocean (6-10%), so more solar energy is absorbed (ice-albedo positive feedback), which melts more ice.

subtopics.title: Point versus non-point sources
subtopics.theory_md:
A **point source** discharges from a single, identifiable, fixed location (pipe, drain, outfall): factory effluent, sewage-plant outfall, power-plant cooling water. It is continuous, easy to measure and control by treatment and discharge standards.

A **non-point (diffused) source** is spread over a large area with no single outlet; rain or irrigation water picks up pollutants as it runs over land: fertiliser and pesticide runoff, urban storm water, construction sediment, acid rain, mining runoff. It is intermittent (rainfall-linked), hard to measure and controlled by land-use management.
subtopics.basics_md: Pollution from one pipe you can point to is a point source. Pollution that arrives from a whole field or city after rain, with no pipe to point at, is non-point.
key_points: Point: single identifiable fixed outlet; non-point: diffuse, large area
Point examples: factory pipe, STP outfall, thermal-plant discharge
Non-point examples: agricultural runoff, urban runoff, acid rain
Point is continuous and easy to monitor and treat; non-point is rainfall-linked and hard to control

subtopics.title: Sources and nature of sewage
subtopics.theory_md:
Major sources of water pollution: **domestic sewage** (organic matter, pathogens, detergent phosphates), **industrial effluents** (heavy metals Hg, Pb, Cd, Cr, acids, alkalis, dyes, oils, toxic organics), **agricultural runoff** (nitrate, phosphate, pesticides), **thermal discharge**, **oil spills**, **mining drainage**, radioactive waste and landfill leachate.

**Domestic sewage** is about 99.9% water, rich in biodegradable organics, N and P, and pathogens, mostly non-toxic and uniform; biological treatment suits it. **Industrial sewage** varies with the industry: toxic, often non-biodegradable (metals, cyanide, phenols, dyes), few pathogens, high COD; it needs pretreatment first.
subtopics.basics_md: Sewage from homes is mostly food, soap and human waste, which microbes can eat. Factory waste can contain metals and chemicals that microbes cannot eat or that even kill them.
key_points: Sources: domestic, industrial, agricultural, thermal, oil spills, mining, radioactive, leachate
Domestic sewage: biodegradable organics, N and P, pathogens, low toxicity
Industrial sewage: toxic, variable, non-biodegradable, high COD, few pathogens
Industrial waste needs pretreatment (neutralisation, metal removal) before biological treatment

topics.topic: Classification and effects of water pollutants

subtopics.title: Classes of water pollutants
subtopics.theory_md:
Water pollutants are classified as:
1. **Organic:** oxygen-demanding wastes (sewage, food, paper; raise BOD), synthetic organics (DDT, detergents, PCBs, phenols), oil.
2. **Inorganic:** heavy metals (Hg, Cd, Pb, As, Cr), acids/alkalis/salts, fluoride (above 1.5 mg/L gives fluorosis).
3. **Plant nutrients:** nitrate, phosphate (eutrophication; blue baby syndrome).
4. **Pathogens:** bacteria, viruses, protozoa (cholera, typhoid, hepatitis); indicator is coliform count.
5. **Sediments and suspended solids** (turbidity).
6. **Radioactive:** $\mathrm{^{90}Sr}$, $\mathrm{^{131}I}$, $\mathrm{^{137}Cs}$.
7. **Thermal** (heat).
subtopics.basics_md: Ask what the pollutant is made of or does: food for microbes (organic), metals and salts (inorganic), fertiliser (nutrients), germs (pathogens), mud (solids), radiation, or heat.

Inorganic: heavy metals, acids/alkalis/salts, fluoride

subtopics.title: Heavy metals and biomagnification
subtopics.theory_md:
**Heavy metals** (Hg, Cd, Pb, As, Cr) and persistent organics (DDT, PCBs) are not metabolised or excreted easily, so they **bioaccumulate** in tissue and **biomagnify**: their concentration rises at each higher trophic level.

Biomagnification needs a pollutant that is **non-biodegradable, fat-soluble and active**. Example (DDT): water 0.000003 ppm, zooplankton 0.04, small fish 0.5, large fish 2, fish-eating birds 25 ppm, a rise of about $8\times10^{6}$ times. DDT thins bird eggshells; methylmercury caused **Minamata disease**; cadmium causes **itai-itai**.
subtopics.basics_md: A fish eats hundreds of small organisms and keeps their poison. A bird eats many fish. So the top animal carries the most.
key_points: Bioaccumulation: build-up in one organism; biomagnification: rise along the food chain
Needs non-biodegradable, fat-soluble pollutant
DDT example with ppm values at each level
Hg: Minamata disease; Cd: itai-itai; DDT: thin eggshells

The birds carry nearly **8 million times** the concentration in water.

subtopics.title: Eutrophication, algal bloom and nitrate
subtopics.theory_md:
**Eutrophication** is enrichment of a water body with N and P (fertiliser runoff, sewage, detergent phosphate). Sequence: nutrients, **algal bloom**, a surface mat that cuts light, death of algae, bacterial decay using up dissolved oxygen (high BOD), **fish kill**, anaerobic $\mathrm{H_2S}$ and $\mathrm{CH_4}$, loss of biodiversity. Warm temperature speeds algal growth and decay, lowers $\mathrm{O_2}$ solubility and causes stratification, so bottom water turns anoxic. Blue-green algae release toxins.

**Blue baby syndrome:** nitrate (above 45 mg/L) is reduced to nitrite in infants; nitrite turns haemoglobin to **methaemoglobin**, which cannot carry $\mathrm{O_2}$.

Prevention: treat sewage with nutrient removal, phosphate-free detergents, balanced fertiliser, buffer strips.
subtopics.basics_md: Fertiliser in water is food for algae. A green mat grows, then dies. Bacteria eat the dead algae and use up the oxygen. The fish then have no air.
key_points: Cause: excess N and P from runoff, sewage, detergents
Chain: bloom, light block, decay, low DO, fish kill
Warm water speeds growth and decay and lowers oxygen solubility
Blue baby: nitrate to nitrite, methaemoglobin, limit 45 mg/L
Prevention: cut nutrient input, buffer strips, remove algae

subtopics.title: Acid mine drainage
subtopics.theory_md:
**Acid mine drainage (AMD)** forms when pyrite $\mathrm{FeS_2}$, exposed by mining, meets air and water:
1. $\mathrm{2FeS_2 + 7O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2Fe^{2+} + 4SO_4^{2-} + 4H^+}$
2. $\mathrm{4Fe^{2+} + O_2 + 4H^+ \rightarrow 4Fe^{3+} + 2H_2O}$ (catalysed by *Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans*)
3. $\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + 3H_2O \rightarrow Fe(OH)_3\downarrow + 3H^+}$ (orange "yellow boy")
4. $\mathrm{FeS_2 + 14Fe^{3+} + 8H_2O \rightarrow 15Fe^{2+} + 2SO_4^{2-} + 16H^+}$

pH falls to 2-4; toxic metals dissolve; fish die. **Limestone** neutralises it: $\mathrm{CaCO_3 + 2H^+ \rightarrow Ca^{2+} + H_2O + CO_2}$, metals precipitate as hydroxides, but $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$ and gypsum coat (**armour**) the stone.
subtopics.basics_md: Mining breaks open rock that contains iron sulphide. Air and rainwater turn it into sulphuric acid, which runs into streams. Limestone is a base, so it eats the acid.
key_points: Pyrite + O2 + water gives Fe2+, sulphate and H+
Fe2+ to Fe3+ (bacterial catalysis), Fe3+ hydrolysis gives Fe(OH)3 and more acid
Fe3+ oxidises more pyrite: self-propagating
Limestone neutralises acid and precipitates metals but gets armoured

subtopics.title: Suspended solids and heat
subtopics.theory_md:
**Suspended solids** (silt, clay, organic matter, algae) cause **turbidity**. Effects: less light so less photosynthesis and DO; organic solids raise BOD; particles clog and abrade fish **gills**; **siltation** buries eggs and bottom organisms; dark particles absorb heat; particles carry adsorbed metals, pesticides and pathogens; reservoirs silt up.

**Heat** is a pollutant (thermal pollution from power-plant cooling water, steel mills, refineries): $\mathrm{O_2}$ solubility falls (about 9.1 mg/L at 20 °C, 7.6 mg/L at 30 °C); metabolism and decay rates rise (about double per 10 °C), so BOD rises when DO is lower; **thermal shock** and loss of spawning; algal blooms; higher toxicity. Control: cooling towers, cooling or spray ponds.
subtopics.basics_md: Mud in water blocks light and clogs gills. Hot water holds less oxygen while fish need more. Both leave water unable to support life.
key_points: Suspended solids: turbidity, less light, gill damage, siltation, carrier of pollutants
Heat lowers DO (9.1 to 7.6 mg/L from 20 to 30 °C)

Control heat by cooling towers/ponds

topics.topic: Prevention and control of water pollution

subtopics.title: Controlling sewage and nutrients
subtopics.theory_md:
Prevention is better than cure: reduce pollution at the source.
- **Treat sewage** (primary, secondary, tertiary with nutrient removal) before discharge; recycle treated water for gardening and industry.
- **Control nutrients:** balanced, need-based fertiliser, organic manure and biofertilisers, phosphate-free detergents, **vegetated buffer strips** along banks.
- **Control non-point runoff** by contour farming and storm-water management.
- **Remedies for a bloom:** remove algae and weeds, aerate, dredge sediment.
- **Law and awareness:** Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974, discharge standards (BOD 30 mg/L), monitoring by CPCB/SPCB.
subtopics.basics_md: Stopping the leak is cheaper than cleaning the lake. Keep fertiliser, sewage and detergent from reaching water, and treat what must be discharged.
key_points: Treat sewage and reuse treated water
Balanced fertiliser, phosphate-free detergent, buffer strips
Control non-point runoff by land-use practices

subtopics.title: Controlling industrial, thermal and oil pollution
subtopics.theory_md:
For industry, treat at the source and before discharge:
- **Neutralise** acidic or alkaline effluent (lime, $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$); **precipitate heavy metals** as hydroxides; remove oil with an API separator; coagulate colloids with alum or $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$.
- **Cleaner production:** reduce, reuse and recycle water; recover materials; **zero liquid discharge** in water-short plants.
- **Thermal:** cool water in **cooling towers or ponds** before release.
- **Oil spills:** booms, skimmers, dispersants.
- **Mining:** limestone treatment and covering pyrite waste to stop acid drainage.
- **Effluent treatment plants (ETP)** and **common effluent treatment plants** for small units.

subtopics.title: Preliminary and primary treatment
subtopics.theory_md:
Plant flow: raw sewage, **screens**, **grit chamber**, **skimming tank**, **primary sedimentation**, **secondary** (ASP or trickling filter), **secondary clarifier**, **tertiary** and disinfection; sludge goes to thickener, **anaerobic digester** and drying beds.

**Preliminary treatment** removes rags, floating objects, grit and oil that would damage pumps, clog pipes and fill tanks. *Screens* remove large floating matter. The *grit chamber* keeps velocity about **0.3 m/s** so sand and gravel settle but organics do not. The *skimming tank* blows air to float oil and grease into side troughs (3-5 min).

**Primary treatment** is physical: **sedimentation** (1.5-2.5 h) removes 50-70% of suspended solids and 25-40% of BOD as primary sludge; scum is skimmed. For industrial waste add equalisation, neutralisation, oil separation, coagulation and metal precipitation.

subtopics.title: Trickling filter
subtopics.theory_md:
A **trickling filter** is a secondary, **attached-growth aerobic** biological reactor, not a strainer. Construction: circular tank, 1-2.5 m of stone or plastic media (25-75 mm), **rotating distributor arm**, **underdrain** with ventilation, effluent channel to the **secondary clarifier**, optional recirculation.

Working: settled sewage is sprayed on the bed and trickles down; a **zoogloeal biofilm** of bacteria, fungi, algae and protozoa adsorbs and oxidises organics with air from the voids: organics + $\mathrm{O_2}$ $\rightarrow$ $\mathrm{CO_2}$ + $\mathrm{H_2O}$ + new cells. Thick film turns anaerobic inside and **sloughs off** to be settled. BOD removal 65-90%.

Merits: simple, low power, shock-resistant. Demerits: odour, filter flies, clogging, large area.
subtopics.basics_md: Imagine stones covered with a slimy layer of microbes. Sewage is sprinkled on top and the microbes eat the dirt as it trickles past, using air that flows through the gaps.
key_points: Attached-growth aerobic biofilm reactor

subtopics.title: Activated sludge, lagoon and comparison
subtopics.theory_md:
**Activated sludge process (ASP)**: suspended-growth aerobic treatment with sludge recycle. Primary effluent is mixed with 20-30% **return activated sludge** in the **aeration tank** (4-8 h, MLSS 1500-3000 mg/L, diffused or mechanical aeration); bacteria oxidise organics; the **secondary clarifier** settles the flocs; part of the sludge is returned, the **excess goes to the digester**. **Aerated lagoon:** earthen basin 2.5-5 m deep with surface aerators, **no sludge recycle**, 3-10 days detention, 70-90% BOD removal, large land, high suspended solids in effluent.

**ASP vs TF:** suspended vs attached growth; forced vs natural aeration; recycle vs none; 85-95% vs 65-90%; small vs large area; high vs low power.

subtopics.title: Aerobic and anaerobic decomposition
subtopics.theory_md:
**Aerobic** (oxygen present; ASP, TF, ponds): organics oxidised to stable products: $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O}$; N goes $\mathrm{NH_3 \rightarrow NO_2^- \rightarrow NO_3^-}$ (*Nitrosomonas*, *Nitrobacter*); S to $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$; P to $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$. Fast, odourless, more sludge.

**Anaerobic** (no oxygen; septic tank, digester): four stages: **hydrolysis**, **acidogenesis**, **acetogenesis**, **methanogenesis**: $\mathrm{CH_3COOH \rightarrow CH_4 + CO_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2 + 4H_2 \rightarrow CH_4 + 2H_2O}$. N goes to $\mathrm{NH_3}$, S to $\mathrm{H_2S}$ (rotten egg smell). Slow, foul, less sludge, gives **biogas** (about 65% $\mathrm{CH_4}$).
subtopics.basics_md: With air, microbes burn waste fully and cleanly. Without air, other microbes break it down in steps and give off smelly gases and methane, which can be used as fuel.

subtopics.title: Sludge treatment and disposal
subtopics.theory_md:
**Sludge** from primary and secondary clarifiers is 95-99% water, putrescible and pathogen-laden. Treatment aims to cut volume, stabilise organics and kill pathogens:
1. **Thickening** (gravity or flotation): solids from about 2% to 5-8%.
2. **Digestion:** **anaerobic digester** at about 35 °C for 15-30 days, giving biogas; aerobic digestion or lime stabilisation as alternatives.
3. **Conditioning** with lime, $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$ or polymer.
4. **Dewatering:** drying beds, centrifuge, filter press (20-40% solids).

**Disposal:** manure/soil conditioner (if metal-free), sanitary landfill, incineration, composting. Ocean dumping is not acceptable.
subtopics.basics_md: Sludge is the thick mud left over after cleaning. It is mostly water and still smelly, so it is thickened, digested to biogas, dried and then used or buried.

subtopics.title: Dissolved oxygen and Winkler's method
subtopics.theory_md:
**Dissolved oxygen (DO)** is molecular $\mathrm{O_2}$ dissolved in water, in mg/L; saturation about 9.1 mg/L at 20 °C and falling with temperature and salinity. Fish need above 4-5 mg/L; low DO means organic pollution.

**Winkler's method:** add $\mathrm{MnSO_4}$ and alkaline KI-azide, then conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$; titrate liberated $\mathrm{I_2}$ with standard thiosulphate (starch indicator).
$\mathrm{2Mn(OH)_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2MnO(OH)_2}$
$\mathrm{MnO(OH)_2 + 4H^+ + 2I^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + I_2 + 3H_2O}$
$\mathrm{I_2 + 2S_2O_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2I^- + S_4O_6^{2-}}$
$$\text{DO (mg/L)} = \frac{V_{thio}\times N\times 8\times 1000}{V_{sample}}$$
subtopics.basics_md: DO tells you how much air fish can breathe. In the test, the oxygen is trapped as a manganese compound, converted to iodine, and the iodine is measured by titration. 8 is the equivalent weight of oxygen.

subtopics.title: BOD and its determination
subtopics.theory_md:
**BOD** is the oxygen (mg/L) needed by aerobic microorganisms to decompose the **biodegradable** organic matter, measured over **5 days at 20 °C in the dark** ($\mathrm{BOD_5}$).

Method: dilute the sample with aerated, nutrient-rich dilution water (seeded if needed); fill two bottles; find DO of one at once ($D_1$, Winkler) and of the other after 5 days ($D_2$).
$$\text{BOD} = \frac{D_1 - D_2}{P},\quad P=\frac{\text{vol. of sample}}{\text{total diluted volume}}$$
Typical values: clean water below 3 mg/L, raw sewage 200-400 mg/L, discharge limit 30 mg/L. Limitations: 5 days, only biodegradable matter, toxins inhibit microbes.
subtopics.basics_md: The more food for microbes in the water, the more oxygen they use up in five days. So oxygen used is a measure of how dirty the water is.

subtopics.title: COD and its determination
subtopics.theory_md:
**COD** is the oxygen equivalent (mg/L) of organic matter oxidised by a strong chemical oxidant, acidic **potassium dichromate**. Method: reflux (open, 2 h) or digest (closed, **150 °C, 2 h**, sealed tube) the sample with a known excess of $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$, conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, $\mathrm{Ag_2SO_4}$ (catalyst) and $\mathrm{HgSO_4}$ (masks $\mathrm{Cl^-}$); run a blank. Back-titrate the leftover dichromate with standard **FAS** using **ferroin** (blue-green to reddish-brown).
$\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_2O}$
$\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 6Fe^{2+} + 14H^+ \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 6Fe^{3+} + 7H_2O}$
$$\text{COD} = \frac{(A-B)\times N\times 8000}{V_{sample}}$$
$A$ = FAS for blank, $B$ = FAS for sample (mL). Closed reflux uses less sample and reagent, less toxic waste, and no loss of volatiles.
subtopics.basics_md: Instead of waiting for microbes, strong chemicals burn all the organic matter in about two hours. The dichromate used up tells how much oxygen would be needed. Blank minus sample, because the sample uses up dichromate.

subtopics.title: Alkalinity and dichromate titration numericals
subtopics.theory_md:
**Alkalinity** is the acid-neutralising capacity of water, due to $\mathrm{OH^-}$, $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$ and $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$, expressed as mg/L of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (eq. wt. 50):
$$\text{Alkalinity} = \text{conc. (mg/L)}\times\frac{50}{\text{eq. wt. of ion}}$$
Equivalent weights: $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$ 60/2 = 30; $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$ 61/1 = 61; $\mathrm{OH^-}$ 17. Convert g/L to mg/L first.

**Redox titration with dichromate:** $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 6Fe^{2+} + 14H^+ \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 6Fe^{3+} + 7H_2O}$, so 1 mol dichromate = **6 mol Fe$^{2+}$**. Moles $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$ = M x V (L); moles Fe = 6 x that; mass = moles x 55.845; % = mass/sample x 100.
